Can You Choose Your Guide in Egypt?

Yes: ask for a specialism, a language, or a man or woman guide, and one certified Egyptologist stays with you throughout. How the matching works

26 November 2026 · 10 minute read

By Islam Hussein, Sillage Égypte journey designer. Last updated: November 2026.

The quick answer

Yes, in the ways that matter. With Sillage Égypte you can ask for a specialism, a language, or a man or woman guide, and one certified Egyptologist then travels with you throughout, from the first day to the last. Your Egyptologist is named in your written proposal before you pay. Where a journey reaches the desert or deep Nubia, a second specialist can join your Egyptologist for those legs.

Key facts

Fact Detail
What can you ask for? A specialism, a language, or a man or woman guide, in your first enquiry
Who stays with you? One certified Egyptologist, from the first day to the last
When will you know the name? In your written proposal, before you pay
What decides the match Language, specialism, and the dates you travel
Second specialist Can join for the desert or deep Nubia, alongside your Egyptologist
Hardest weeks to match Christmas and New Year, and the week of the 2 August 2027 eclipse
Cost No extra cost unless it is shown in your proposal

In Egypt, the guide is the experience. The temples have pointed the same way for three and a half thousand years; what varies is the person standing beside you, reading them. Most travellers spend longer choosing a hotel than choosing the voice their Egypt will arrive in. This post answers the two questions discerning travellers ask Sillage Égypte (sillage-egypte.com), the private Egypt journey designer: what can you ask for in a guide, and will one person stay with you the whole way. Every Sillage journey is private throughout (your own car, your own certified Egyptologist, someone who can read the walls, not recite a script), so the guide is settled when the journey is designed, not at the airport. What an Egyptologist actually is (the training, the licence, what a doctorate adds) is the subject of our pillar guide.

Can I choose my guide for an Egypt trip?

Yes: you choose what kind of guide you travel with, and we match the person. Every journey is designed around the people travelling, and the guide is part of the design, not a staffing decision made the week before you fly. There are three things to ask for:

You can ask for What it means An example
A specialism The subject your journey turns on The New Kingdom tombs, Nubian history, Islamic Cairo
A language The language you want your Egypt told in Say which one, and you will hear whether it can be matched
A man or woman guide Your preference, simply part of the match Say so in your enquiry; a woman guide is available on request

The request is made in the enquiry itself. Your journey designer then checks it against your dates and names your Egyptologist in the written proposal, so you see who you are travelling with before you pay. Most travellers arrive with a fascination rather than a brief (Coptic Egypt, the New Kingdom tombs, the desert), and the designer translates that fascination into the right person.

Notes on what to ask for

  • Ask what a guide studies, not how many journeys they have led. On a wall that rewards depth, a researcher serves you better than a raconteur.
  • Name the fascination, and let the designer do the matching.
  • Decide on language early. A guide working in a language you think in, rather than one you translate through, changes how much stays with you at the tomb door.
  • Calendars are the quiet constraint. Every guide has a finite number of weeks a year, and the weeks everyone wants go first.

Will I have the same guide for the whole trip?

Yes. One certified Egyptologist travels with you from the first day to the last: the person who starts with you in Cairo is the person at the temple door in Luxor, and at the temples of Abu Simbel. This is stated Sillage practice, and it follows directly from the model: every journey is private throughout, with no scheduled departures and no shared groups. The guide is not assigned to your booking; the guide is part of it.

Continuity changes the quality of the guiding itself. A guide who has travelled with you for three days knows you take the long tomb and skip the alabaster shop, that you photograph doorways, that midday belongs to shade; by day five the explanations have become a conversation rather than a commentary. On many shared-coach itineraries the guide changes with the region, Cairo handing you to Luxor, Luxor to Aswan. That is logistics, not a failure; it is simply a different product. The private model keeps one reader of walls beside you while the walls change around them.

There is a practical dividend too: timing. Because your Egyptologist travels with you rather than meeting you, the day bends (the Valley of the Kings at first opening, a slower afternoon when the heat asks for one), shaped by someone standing next to you, not by a timetable in a head office.

How does the matching work: language, specialism, dates?

Three filters decide the match: the language you want your Egypt told in, the specialism your journey implies, and the dates you travel. All three are settled in the design conversation, before any day-by-day is final.

Language comes first, because everything else builds on it. Say which language you need, and you will hear plainly whether it can be matched for your dates. Language is not a detail of the booking; it is the medium your whole journey arrives in.

Specialism is the second filter. A journey shaped around Islamic Cairo and the oases asks for one kind of reader, a New Kingdom deep-dive on the west bank at Luxor another, and a journey that turns south of Aswan another again. The specialism is what you are really choosing when you choose a guide.

A preference for a man or woman guide sits alongside these. A woman guide is available on request, and it is simply part of the match rather than a special case.

Dates are the honest constraint. A guiding calendar is finite, and some weeks are crowded before they begin: Christmas and New Year behaves that way, and so will 2 August 2027, when a total solar eclipse crosses Egypt, with totality of about six minutes and twenty seconds at Luxor. For those weeks, make your request when you first ask about the journey; Christmas in Egypt and the 2027 eclipse are the two calendars worth reading before you write.

When does a second specialist join the journey?

On two kinds of ground, a second specialist can join your party for those legs: the desert, and the deep south. They join your Egyptologist rather than replace them; the Egyptologist who started with you stays with you. This is the part of the matching that a shared schedule cannot offer: holding a second expert for one travelling party is a matter of design, not logistics.

The desert legs bring the mechanics of a desert journey, the reading of that landscape, the judgement the wilderness asks for. The southern legs (Aswan and Nubia, Abu Simbel) bring Nubian history. Abu Simbel read by someone who studies it is a different temple from Abu Simbel read from a laminated card.

The design logic is continuity plus depth. One Egyptologist keeps the thread of your journey from the first day to the last, and where the ground changes character entirely, a specialist in that ground can arrive for those days. The clearest example is Beyond the Nile, a 16-day journey at €11,650 per person for two or more that crosses Cairo, Alexandria, Siwa and the Great Sand Sea before six nights on the Oberoi Zahra from Aswan to Luxor, with Abu Simbel reached by air: the one shape where both kinds of ground appear in a single journey. Any cost for a second specialist is shown in your proposal; if it is not shown, there is none.

How do you ask for the guide you want with Sillage?

Name the specialism, the language or the preference in your enquiry; everything after that is conversation.

  1. Note what you want to understand, the language you want it in, and any preference for a man or woman guide.
  2. Send a sentence through Plan your journey, free and without obligation, with your dates, your party and your request.
  3. A named journey designer replies within 24 hours and checks your request against your dates before shaping the private itinerary around you.
  4. Refine the proposal together (pace adjusted, the day-by-day argued over), with your Egyptologist named in it. Then a 25% non-refundable deposit secures the booking. The balance is due 60 days before arrival, or in full if you book inside 60 days, and the price is fixed once Sillage confirms in writing, except for government action, taxes and fees, or significant currency changes.

Honest counsel on who this is for. A precise request suits returning visitors and travellers with a specific fascination: a second journey to the Valley of the Kings, a year of reading Coptic history, a desert already dreamt about. If this is your first Egypt journey and no specialism yet has hold of you, do not agonise; tell us what drew you to Egypt and trust the match. And if the guide who fits your request is busy on your dates, you are told plainly and we propose the nearest match or a small shift of your dates. There is no quiet swap.

FAQ

Can I request a female guide in Egypt? Yes. Sillage can provide a woman guide on request, and the preference is simply part of the match rather than a special case. Name it in your enquiry and the designer builds around it.

Can I ask for a particular guide by name? We match on specialism, language and your preference for a man or woman guide rather than from a published list of names. Your Egyptologist is then named in your written proposal before you pay, so you know who you are travelling with.

Do Sillage guides speak languages other than English? Language is treated as a first filter in matching rather than an afterthought. Say which language you want your Egypt told in, and you will hear plainly whether it can be matched for your dates.

What happens if the right guide is not free on my dates? The designer tells you plainly and proposes the nearest match or a small shift of your dates. There is no quiet swap. Nothing is booked and nothing is owed until a deposit is paid; the enquiry is free, without obligation, and a real person replies within 24 hours.

How far ahead should I make my request? For most weeks of the year, a few months ahead is comfortable. For Christmas and New Year, make it when the journey is first discussed, nine to twelve months out. For the eclipse week of 2 August 2027 in Luxor, enquire now.

Does asking for a particular kind of guide cost more? No, unless an extra cost is shown in your proposal. The proposal prices the private journey as a whole, and once confirmed in writing the price is fixed, except for government action, taxes and fees, or significant currency changes. A 25% non-refundable deposit secures the booking; the balance is due 60 days before arrival.

The takeaway

You can choose the kind of guide you travel with in Egypt: a specialism, a language, a man or woman guide. One certified Egyptologist stays with you from the first day to the last, with a second specialist able to join where the desert or Nubia asks for one. Send one sentence through Plan your journey, naming the fascination; a journey designer replies within 24 hours.
